articles.title_orig: China’s Companionship Economy: Paying for Someone to Play With Me - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: China’s Companionship Economy: Paying for Someone to Play With Me - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
I’ve been playing computer games since I was a kid, so when “Shift at Midnight” came out in August and quickly became one of the hottest games on social media, I had to give it a try. It is a cooperative horror game in which players work the night shift at a supermarket. Players have to identify customers who are monsters in disguise, keep the supermarket running, and, of course, fight the monsters after nightfall. According to the game developers, this game is best suited for three players, so I needed two teammates.
The easy option would be to find teammates in the game lobby. But as an introvert and also not-so-skilled player, I feel very reluctant to team up with strangers. In team games, a simple mistake can lead to failures and that means upsetting other players. Teammates easily lose patience and start pressuring each other. I hate the blaming and yelling; they really take all the fun out of the game.
So I found my teammates another way. I decided to hire two gaming companions through DONGDONG E-GAME, a platform dedicated to this type of gaming companion service that I had come across through their livestreams and promo videos on social media. I paid around 40 to 50 yuan ($6-7) per person per hour. They both seemed to be recent college graduates. And judging from our in-game conversation, I think they were treating this as a full-time job.
Our game lasted five hours. I got to play at the checkout, where I tried to identify suspicious customers; this was the most fun part of the game. My companions took care of cleaning, stocking goods, and most of the fighting. One was particularly familiar with the game and knew where the monsters would appear. He would warn me before the more frightening scenes.
After hours spotting monsters and fighting spiders, we finally reached the big boss, and I died within seconds (in my defense, that was one hell of a boss fight). They finished the fight while I sat and watched our battle. The game ended. We had earned enough money to save our pet cat, one of the desired outcomes, but we failed to save a police officer who was eventually killed by the monster. This is one of the “bad endings,” but I was okay with it.
Paying for someone to play a video game with you may sound strange. I also imagine many people would laugh at the idea of taking on this kind of work as a career.
How much you pay really depends on the type of gaming companion you want. There are two types: skill-based companionship and entertainment companionship. Skill-based companionship is for people who want a skilled teammate to help them win or achieve a particular objective. If they lose or fail to achieve the objective then they will give a conditional refund or some make-up sessions. For the more popular competitive games such as “Delta Force” or “Valorant,” I’ve seen hourly rates ranging from 60 yuan to as high as 500 yuan, depending on the skill of the player and the nature of the service.
Entertainment companionship is for people who just want some company, some light chatting, and an enjoyable gaming experience. That’s exactly what I got in my paid session.
When Intimacy Becomes the Product
Gaming companions make some sense to me. The session has clear goals: to win a game or at least enjoy the game. But there are other types of paid companions in today’s Chinese society, with more focus on intimacy.
One good example is lianpei , paid love role-playing games , which is a niche product in the bigger sector of jubensha , the immersive role-playing games popular among Chinese young people for quite some time. A typical romance role-play session normally involves six to 10 people, including one or two dungeon masters (DMs).  The rest are players who pay to participate. DMs are performers hired by the venue to perform roles and interact with players. The game enacts romance stories filled with passion, jealousy, separation, and reconciliation. There is limited physical intimacy such as holding hands and hugging, or maybe a light kiss on the forehead.
A classical immersive role-playing game session usually costs a little over 100 yuan per person, but romantic role-play sessions can easily cost 200 to 300 yuan per person or more. Some players said they have spent over 1,000 yuan to make one session happen.
As anyone can easily imagine, DMs are usually good looking charming young people, and popular ones can easily attract their own fans. Players need to secure booking weeks or even months in advance, and sometimes they need to pay extra for it. In some extreme cases, players would cover most or even the entire cost of the group to make sure they can book the script and the DM they want. This reminds me of idol culture in Asia. Idols’ popularity usually depends on their interaction and connections with fans.
In August 2026, Chinese media reported a very concerning case involving lianpei. A 16-year-old girl in Shanghai reportedly spent around 170,000 yuan on romantic role-play sessions. According to the news report, she had booked hundreds of sessions at the same venue over the last two years. Her family accused the venue of encouraging her to keep spending.
This is an extreme case, but it reveals how much greed and tragedy can be associated with this type of transaction. Both gaming companions and DMs tend to describe what they do as a service. They make this sound like a very strict business transaction, where customers pay for and receive a specific service.
However, feelings are never that simple and straightforward; they are unpredictable and sometimes stubborn. On a rational level, the players know this is a scripted love session that they paid money to join. They know the person playing their lover or friend is just doing their job, and still, players fall for them from time to time, over and over again.
The Business of Being Wanted
Attempting to purchase intimacy is not new. Paying for companionship, sex, matchmaking, and the attention of others is a phenomenon as old as recorded history. The psychology behind these transactions is actually quite simple. We want to feel wanted and we want to believe that we are special to someone. We want to feel loved.
In Chinese classical literature, many stories about courtesans and their patrons share this theme. They tend to examine the thin lines between money, sex, and genuine affection. A recurring theme is that what begins as a transaction might eventually lead to true love. In a very well-known Ming Dynasty story, the heroine Du Shiniang, a young courtesan, falls in love with a young man who has a promising career. Du intends to leave the brothel and start a new life with him. When another man comes along and offers money for her however, her lover immediately agrees to sell her.
The story ends in tragedy, with Du Shiniang throwing her treasure chest into the river and ending her own life. She genuinely believed she could walk away from her past and that her lover was actually in love with her – not her reputation, not her money, but her as a person. In the end, however, he felt money mattered the most.
The story may be hundreds of years old but the core theme still resonates. The quest for true affection has not stopped; on the contrary, now in the internet age, with the help of new technology, this age-old search is taking new commercial forms. On Chinese streaming platforms such as Douyin and Kuaishou, many talented (or not) hosts sing, dance, or simply chat with viewers, hoping to receive virtual gifts. In a random group hosts’ livestream, I have seen one viewer sending ten Carnivals (worth 3,000 yuan each) in just five seconds.
This is also where things can become very ugly. Some livestreaming hosts actively encourage these gifts, and imply to viewers that spending more will bring them closer. The viewers keep spending money, hoping to prove that their relationship means something more than business. articles.title_orig: Dow futures soar 1,000 points as big midterm wins by Democrats remove political uncertainty risk on Wall Street: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow futures soar 1,000 points as big midterm wins by Democrats remove political uncertainty risk on Wall Street: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Democrats decisively took control of Congress Tuesday night, delivering a stinging rebuke to President Donald Trump and his economic record as voters voiced deep frustration with rising prices, government corruption and the AI data center build-out .
The party scored an extraordinary pair of victories in traditionally Republican Texas. James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton, becoming the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from the state in nearly four decades. Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term Gov. Greg Abbott, making her the first Democratic governor of Texas since Ann Richards left office in 1995. Texas became the clearest measure of how far the blue wave reached: Democrats swept the state's marquee races in a Republican stronghold long considered beyond their grasp.
Follow CNBC's live coverage of the 2026 midterm election results
The victories were part of a broader wave of Democratic gains. In South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews upset Darline Graham in a race Republicans had expected to win. In Ohio, Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Sen. Jon Husted. Democrats also flipped Senate seats in Iowa and North Carolina and won key races in Georgia and New Hampshire.
The results marked a striking collapse for Trump's candidates. Paxton, Graham and Husted were among the president's prominent picks who lost after he made dozens of endorsements.
The election also sharpened the political fight over data centers and artificial intelligence infrastructure . Texas is a major center of planned data-center construction , and Hinojosa campaigned for a pause on new projects until the state adopts tougher rules. Her victory gives Democrats more influence over Texas' approach to the build-out, though the state Legislature remains in Republican hands.
The results also delivered a blow to the tech billionaires and corporate interest groups that poured hundreds of millions of dollars into backing Republican candidates who might be friendly to the massive AI data center projects they hope to build around the country. Elon Musk, the world's richest man and the cycle's largest individual political donor, spent record sums in a failed effort to help Republicans retain power, including in Texas.
Musk's spending may have become a liability as voters raised concerns about government corruption and the growing influence of billionaires in exit polls. Talarico repeatedly attacked Musk on the campaign trail, accusing him of trying to buy "his very own personal United States Senator."
"Tonight's results are a wake-up call for corporate special interests and billionaires who have been rigging the economy," said Rep. Chris Pappas, who defeated former Republican Sen. John Sununu to win an open Senate seat in New Hampshire.
The outcome is poised to reshape the technology sector's relationship with Washington. A more adversarial Congress is likely to intensify scrutiny of tech companies and the AI data center build-out. Markets reacted as the scale of Democratic gains became clear: Dow futures fell and S&P 500 futures slipped Tuesday evening.
Economic frustration was also central to Democratic gains. Many voters blamed Trump's tariffs and the war with Iran for worsening their economic situation, while the cost of living remained a persistent strain.
Democratic control of both chambers gives the party a powerful check on Trump in the final two years of his term, including the ability to block parts of his agenda and intensify congressional oversight. The results sent a clear warning: promises to bring down costs did not overcome voters' frustration with prices, corruption and the country's direction.
Silicon Valley spent record sums trying to shape the election. Instead, it got a Democratic House promising to haul its CEOs before congressional investigators.
Many of the winners ran against not just Trump, but the billionaire donors who helped bankroll Republicans. In North Carolina, Cooper told supporters that North Carolinians "will always matter more than the billionaires and the insiders."
In Texas, Talarico defeated Paxton despite more than $200 million from SpaceX CEO Musk to stop him. On the same ballot, Hinojosa defeated Abbott after blaming him for the rapid buildout of data centers across Texas, saying the governor for putting Big Tech interests ahead of local communities.
The GOP had a commanding advantage among the election's biggest donors. According to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records, 14 of the 20 largest donor groups backed Republicans exclusively or nearly so. Crypto, AI, and online gambling interests poured more than $377 million into races.
Not all of Silicon Valley's money ended up on the losing side. LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman, one of Democrats' biggest donors, cast the results as "an overwhelming wave against Trump and his cronies" and took a direct shot at Musk.
"We should get money out of politics," Hoffman wrote on X late Tuesday. "And while people like Elon are spending outrageous amounts to keep authoritarian clowns in power, those of us who believe in the ideals of America cannot yield."
With control of the House comes the power to launch investigations, issue subpoenas and examine the Trump administration and its allies. That's going to be a challenge for tech companies to navigate as they find themselves in Democratic crosshairs.
Democrats are already calling for AI executives to testify under oath.
Among the first to seize on the results was Rep. Greg Casar, the Texas Democrat who chairs the Congressional Progressive Caucus.
"The House Democratic majority must make it a top priority to protect Americans' jobs, freedom, and lives from AI billionaires," Casar said in a statement after Democrats were projected to win the House. "AI company CEOs should be called to testify under oath."
Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the presumptive next chair of the oversight committee, put it more simply: "Lawyer up," he said in a statement.
The results also present headwinds for the infrastructure undergirding AI.
The Texas results appear to be a warning sign for the AI industry in a state projected to overtake Virginia as the world's biggest data center market by 2030, according to JLL . Abbott had long courted data center development before shifting his position this year as the backlash grew. Talarico and Hinojosa both seized on that anger, winning over Republican voters fed up with data centers going up in their communities. Hinojosa has promised to force lawmakers to regulate the industry .
In a CNBC Voter Poll, 56% of voters said data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision, with Democrats ranking the issue higher than Republicans.
Trump personally pushed states to redistrict their congressional seats mid-decade to cement a Republican majority in the House. The effort largely flopped.
Many of the GOP's redrawn districts ended up falling to Democrats, despite the unprecedented effort to defend or flip them by redrawing boundaries mid-decade.
That includes seats in Texas, Florida and North Carolina, which Democrats won despite Republicans making them safer. In Texas, where Republicans began their redistricting war that then spread to other states, Democrats ended up winning most of the gerrymandered seats.
The redistricting push was always risky because no recent census was available when the maps were drawn.
Trump rolled out the red carpet for Paxton, only for Republicans to lose a Senate seat in Texas for the first time in over three decades.
Talarico's victory in Texas came after Trump endorsed Paxton over the incumbent Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who held the seat for decades. In endorsing Paxton, Trump said Cornyn had not been sufficiently loyal.
Paxton prevailed in a bitter primary, and Trump's move to tip the scales spurned Senate Republicans, who saw Cornyn as a better and less expensive candidate than Paxton — who had a laundry list of scandals that plagued his campaign.

articles.title_orig: Israel’s president accepts certified election results in a blow to Netanyahu's claim of vote fraud
articles.title_zh: Israel’s president accepts certified election results in a blow to Netanyahu's claim of vote fraud
articles.content_orig:
Nov. 4 (UPI) -- Israeli election officials on Wednesday narrowly certified the results of the country's inconclusive general election, a week after Israelis voted in what was widely seen as a referendum of the leadership of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and in particular his handling of the Oct. 7 attacks in 2023.
At a ceremony at which the Israeli president officially adopted the results from the Central Elections Committee, President Isaac Herzog said he would later Wednesday begin the consultation process on which leader among the various Knesset blocs should be invited to form a new government .
He warned compromise was critical in order to avoid new elections and that the various blocs vying to form a government would not be able to deliver on every campaign "commitment and promise," urging them instead to demonstrate "originality, creativity, courage and goodwill" in the interests of the country.
"The one test I ask the factions and their representatives to keep in front of them when they come here is this: what is truly best for the country," said Herzog.
The ceremony went ahead after the committee voted 15-14 , with two abstentions, to approve the election results, prompting CEC chair Noam Sohlberg to warn that the level of opposition within the committee "sets a dangerous precedent."
Herzog also expressed "full confidence" in Shin Bet, Israel's domestic intelligence agency, to get to the bottom of fraud allegations leveled against political parties that represent Israeli-Palestinians after they won a record 19 Knesset seats, but hit out against what he called "coarse" and "racist" attacks on the country's Arab minority.
His comments came after Sohlberg pushed back against efforts by Netanyahu's Likud Party to delay certification of the election due to the cheating allegations, warning that efforts to call into question the integrity of the results constituted a "real danger" to Israel's democracy and that even if fraud had occurred, it would not have materially affected the outcome.
Solhberg said it was impossible to postpone publication of the results on the basis of what were suspicions only, because it would entail extending the term of a Knesset whose term had already ended.
"Accordingly, we publish the elections now. If evidence is found going forward, it will be possible to act on the path set out by law for appealing the election results," he added.

articles.title_orig: World reacts to Democrats’ midterm elections victory
articles.title_zh: World reacts to Democrats’ midterm elections victory
articles.content_orig:
The White House is illuminated in Washington, Tuesday. Alex Brandon/AP hide caption
One color dominates international headlines about the U.S. midterm election results . French newspaper Libération called the Democrats' win " une vague bleue ," or blue wave, Britain's Daily Mail dubbed it a "historic blue tsunami," and The Times of India's headline ran "midterm blues for Trump."
Countries at war were also watching closely, with Ukrainian newspaper The Kyiv Independent's online headline hopeful : "Democrats seize control of Congress in blow to Trump, potential boost for Ukraine."
Russia had a different take. Rossiyskaya Gazeta , the state-run daily newspaper, suggested the results would in fact be a blow to Ukraine, which has firm support from the European Union. "Brussels, brace yourself. After the Republicans' defeat, Trump's wrath will fall on Europe," read the headline.
In the Middle East, the Tehran Times put the Republicans' resounding defeat down to President Trump's decision to attack Iran earlier this year.
"The Iran war comes home to hit Trump at the ballot box," its headline read. The war, which Trump promised would be over quickly, has dragged on, sent oil prices soaring, and affected many Americans' daily lives with the affordability crisis.
And in Israel, which just held its own seismic elections last week, headlines focused on what the Democrats' victory means for the U.S. support of the Jewish state and its war in Gaza.
The Times of Israel ran a headline focusing on Democrat, and Muslim, candidate Abdul El-Sayed's triumph in the Michigan Senate race, saying "Anti-Israel El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate race, pledges no money for 'apartheid, genocide.'" The headline in Israel's other daily Haaretz read: "Abdul El-Sayed Shows Opposition to Israel Is No Barrier to Winning Battleground States."
Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks at an election night event, early Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, in Detroit. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP hide caption
The Toronto Star in Canada, which is in the midst of a contentious trade war with the U.S., called the results a "rebuke" to Trump. Across the southern border in Mexico, El Universal newspaper's headline was similar, reading simply: "Setback for Trump."
Many foreign leaders shied away from commenting directly on the results, as unlike a U.S. presidential election where they politely congratulate the winner, they see midterms as a domestic American issue.
However Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has an acrimonious relationship with Trump, was forthright on X.
"Yesterday, American society voted against policies that only impoverish. Against hate. Against machismo. Against climate denialism and against the privileges of the elites," Sánchez said.
In South Africa, where diplomatic relations with the U.S. are at an all-time low after Trump falsely accused the government of persecuting its white minority, President Cyril Ramaphosa said "The people of America have spoken."
Ramaphosa made the comments as he cast his own ballot in South Africa's municipal elections Wednesday, adding: "I do think that this is going to introduce a new era in world relations…. We're hoping that on a bilateral basis there will be a coming together of minds."
A senior Russia diplomat suggested the Democratic Party's return to power in both houses of Congress bode ill for U.S.-Russian relations. "The approach of the activist wing of the Democratic Party towards Russia is extremely negative. There's nothing new in that," said Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov in an interview with the state RIA-Novosti news service. Ryabkov also signaled there would be no grand shifts in Russian foreign policy as a result.
In Germany, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius congratulated Democrats on an "historic victory," adding that Berlin's commitment to cooperating with the administration in Washington remains unchanged. He stressed that Berlin will be reaching out to both Democrats and Republicans.
Iranian government supporters step on U.S. and Israeli flags during the annual rally marking the anniversary of the 1979 U.S. Embassy takeover, outside the former embassy in Tehran, Iran, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. Vahid Salemi/AP hide caption
Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere said the results are a "powerful political signal about a change of course among American voters." Speaking to Reuters, Stoere said "voices are now emerging in American politics that are closer to us than the president and the administration have stood for, for example on climate and environment, and in foreign policy and development aid policy."
There was no immediate reaction from UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, but London Mayor Sadiq Khan, who Trump has frequently sparred with, said on X: "Congratulations to Democrats on a huge victory last night. With a focus on hope, unity and supporting families with the cost of living - their campaign was a true rejection of the damaging and divisive politics of Donald Trump."
A spokeswoman for China's foreign ministry told a daily press conference that the midterm elections "are an internal affair of the United States." She added that "China is willing to continue working with the U.S. to…strengthen communication, properly manage differences, expand cooperation, and build a constructive, strategically stable China-U.S. relationship based on the principles of respect, fairness, and reciprocity."
Japan's top government spokesman, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told a press conference that Japan's alliance with the U.S. remains essential for global peace and stability, regardless of the outcome of midterm elections.
The alliance "remains the cornerstone of Japan's foreign and security policy" and is crucial to "maximizing its national interests" amid an increasingly volatile and uncertain global situation," he added.
Iran's Parliament Speaker and top negotiator Mohammad ‌Baqer Ghalibaf commented on X: "Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message. If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare."
For Israel, the US midterm results fall during a time of political uncertainty, amid coalition-building talks after Trump's ally, incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, lost his parliamentary majority in Oct. 27 Israeli elections. "In some ways Netanyahu lost two elections in the last week," said Israel-American analyst Mairav Zonstein.
Netanyahu's rivals seized on the midterm results. One Israeli opposition leader, Yair Golan, said the U.S. results reveal "just how toxic Netanyahu is among both Democrats and Republicans." Another, Yair Lapid, said the U.S. results "eliminate any possibility of a unity government led by Netanyahu."
Additional reporting by Charles Maynes in Moscow, Esme Nicholson in Berlin, Lauren Frayer in Tel Aviv, Hadeel Al-Shalchi in Istanbul, Anthony Kuhn in Seoul.

articles.title_orig: Switch 1 & 2 Cartridges Under Threat As Key ROM Manufacturer Exits Business
articles.title_zh: Switch 1 & 2 Cartridges Under Threat As Key ROM Manufacturer Exits Business
articles.content_orig:
Macronix, one of Nintendo's key ROM manufacturers for physical game cartridges, is ceasing the production of ROM altogether.
This comes via analyst David Gibson who relayed the news from Macronix's latest financial release. According to the data, ROM products accounted for just 5% of the firm's overall revenue for Q3 2026, representing a stark decrease of 39% year-on-year.
It will now shift its focus over to NOR and eMMC memory chips instead, and will no longer report ROM sales separately in its future financial releases.
Gibson is keen to stress that Nintendo will have other partners to utilise when it comes to the production of cartridges, but this move may nevertheless accelerate the transition to digital game sales alongside Game-Key Cards.
Digital sales have already made up more than 60% of Nintendo's total sales during Q4 2026 and Q1 2027, but this tends to fluctuate based on major game releases.
It'll be interesting to see whether Nintendo itself addresses this development in its own financial release, which it due to drop this week on 5th November. Even if it doesn't acknowledge it in its own material, it seems likely that the question will arise in the company's usual Q&A session. We'll keep an eye out and relay its reaction and plans going forward.
For now, it's likely business as usual for Nintendo, but we'll be interested to see just how this affects the production of physical cartridges in the future and whether it will indeed accelerate the transition to digital.

articles.title_orig: CVS to Split Off Pharmacy Business, Ending the Healthcare Conglomerate Era
articles.title_zh: CVS to Split Off Pharmacy Business, Ending the Healthcare Conglomerate Era
articles.content_orig:
CVS Health said Wednesday it is splitting into two companies, marking one of the largest shakeups in the healthcare industry. It’s a major reversal of the mergers that brought together the nation’s largest drugstore retailer along with health insurance giant Aetna and pharmacy benefit manager Caremark.
The breakup unwinds a strategy that began in 2007, when CVS merged with Caremark, which handles prescription benefits available to people with health insurance. In 2018, CVS acquired Aetna for $69 billion.
“We’re basically taking what I believe is one great company and making it two,” said CEO David Joyner in a statement.
Shares of CVS Health, which had been up about 15% so far this year, fell by 2% in premarket trading after initially ticking up. Shareholders will get shares of both companies in a tax-free transaction expected to close in early 2028, according to the company.
CVS also reported higher third-quarter earnings and revenue Wednesday, due primarily to better results from its Health Care Benefits segment. The company also raised its earnings guidance for the rest of this year.
CVS has 9,000 locations across the United States, 800 of which operate “MinuteClinics” staffed by nurse practitioners and physician assistants.

McDonald's ( MCD ) sales growth slowed in the third quarter as consumers faced a challenging economic backdrop and the fast food chain unveiled its growth strategy. The results showed that same-store sales grew by 1.5% year over year, a tick above the 1.4% growth Wall Street expected, according to Bloomberg estimates. In Q3 last year, McDonald's posted same-store sales growth of 3.6%.
In the US, the company posted a 0.2% decline in comparable sales, slightly narrower than the expected 0.5% drop. Data from Placer.ai showed visits to the Golden Arches declined from a year ago, but the company said customers spent more when they did go. Promotions in October led to some strength ahead of the holiday season. CEO Chris Kempczinski said the company is "encouraged by improvement as the quarter progressed following our intervention on value."
Revenue came in at nearly $7.2 billion, below expectations of $7.4 billion, alongside adjusted earnings of $3.57 per share, above the expected $3.40 per share.
Ahead of the results, BTIG analyst Peter Saleh said "lower-income challenges, disappointing promotions and overly crowded marketing calendars" were top concerns among franchisee operators in the quarter.
"Beverages were called out as a rare bright spot," he added, alluding to an energy drink McDonald's launched with Red Bull in September.
The company is also leaning into holiday offerings beginning on Nov. 3. McDonald's unveiled a limited-time lineup consisting of a cookie butter coffee or latte, a cranberry-infused Sprite drink, and a cranberry-flavored Red Bull energy drink.
Citi's Jon Tower shared a similar message in a note, writing, "We still have confidence in beverages as a broader platform, [and] another attempt at entry-level value should come in early '27."
The company named Skye Anderson, a 26-year McDonald's veteran, as president of McDonald's USA last quarter. Anderson is working on a new value menu for 2027 after franchisees and consumers didn't fully engage with the company's under-$3 offerings.
Anderson will play a key role in a new growth strategy as McDonald's makes a long-term bet on artificial intelligence, hand-breaded chicken, and a return of the 90s-style restaurant design to regain customers who left for other chains, like Burger King ( QSR ).
McDonald's said it plans to invest $8.5 billion through 2036 to support restaurant tech updates with rent relief and capital. It intends to deliver roughly $5 billion of that investment by 2030.
According to Saleh, franchisees' reactions to the NEXT growth strategy are mixed.
"Franchisees [are] highly skeptical that level of margin gain is possible, unconvinced a broad remodel program is needed, and noting very few details about cost and co-investment have been shared," Saleh wrote. "Without a significant reduction in build cost and more field-testing, we don't believe Project NEXT can proceed."
McDonald's operators are expected to update the restaurants' look and feel as part of a 10-year remodel cycle, per McDonald's, and Kempczinski said those costs typically add up to $400,000 to $450,000 per restaurant.
Deploying the suite of McDonald's productivity improvements will cost franchise operators an additional $800,000 per US restaurant. For international markets, it will run operators around $650,000 to $750,000.

Election Day has nearly come to an end, with tens of millions of voters having flocked to the polls around the U.S. Through a series of stunning victories, Democrats have been projected to take back control of both chambers of Congress .
Many key races that fell in favor of Democrats were called on Tuesday night, including wins in Texas , Kansas , South Carolina , Iowa , and more. Other, tighter contests could take multiple days—if not longer—to determine a winner. It all boils down to the states, which the U.S. Constitution empowers to establish the times, places, and manners of holding elections and counting ballots.
Certain states are known for having shorter count times, such as Florida. Others typically take longer, like California, due to its size, and Alaska, where ranked-choice voting can make the process of certifying votes more complicated.
“There are all these differences, both in process and deadlines, and geography, and who the voters are, and who the candidates are, that make a difference in what this looks like,” Mitchell Brown, a professor of political science at Auburn University and the author of “How We Vote: Innovations in American Elections,” tells TIME.
Read more: The Key Congressional Races to Watch on Election Night
Mitchell says that it could take up to 30 days before all the states certify their results. She stresses that official midterm results released by the states themselves are different from projections from media outlets, which will call races sooner.
“It's really important for everyone to understand that what happens on election night when we're watching TV or looking online, and we're seeing races called, those are predictions by media outlets. They're not the official results,” adds Chris Mann, the research director at The Center for Election Innovation & Research. “With close elections, we may end up not knowing who the winner is until we get to those official certifications that every vote has been counted.”
Here’s what to know about how the midterm votes will be tabulated, and when we are likely to know the results.
Polls open and close at varying times in different states around the country, with most closing their polls around 7 p.m. or 8 p.m. local time. Because the U.S. is divided across several time zones, however, those closures are spread over several hours on Election Day. And in some cases closing times vary even between different parts of the same state.
Here is when the latest polls close in each of the 50 states and Washington, D.C., in Eastern Standard Time.
7 p.m. EST : Georgia, Indiana, Kentucky, South Carolina, Vermont, and Virginia.
7:30 p.m. EST : Ohio and West Virginia.
North Carolina also typically closes its final polls at this time, but due to minor technical issues reported in some localities on Tuesday—which have since been resolved—the state’s board of elections has extended voting hours in some precincts.
8 p.m. EST : Alabama, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Oklahoma, Rhode Island, Tennessee, and Washington, D.C.
In Pennsylvania, most polling sites will close at 8 p.m., but in three precincts they will stay open for an additional half hour “due to machine set-up issues” that delayed the opening of those polls this morning, according to Chester County officials.
Read more: The 7 Key Governor Races to Watch in the Midterm Elections
9 p.m. EST : Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, North Dakota, South Dakota, Texas, Wisconsin, and Wyoming.
10 p.m. EST : Montana, Nevada, and Utah.
11 p.m. EST : California, Idaho, Oregon, and Washington state.
After their respective polls close, states must verify and count ballots that were cast in various ways, including those made in person during the early voting period and on Election Day, mail-in ballots, and provisional ballots.
Depending on the state, ballots are either counted right at voting locations, or transported back to county counting facilities. Mann says these facilities are like warehouses containing machines that can quickly and accurately count votes.
Read more: 8 Senate Races the Forecasters Can’t Agree On
Provisional ballots allow people to vote who fail to meet certain eligibility requirements that can later be verified. If, for example, someone arrives at a polling site and does not have their ID, they may be able to vote through a provisional ballot that can then be counted if and when they have verified their identity.
Brown says the process of confirming provisional ballots is called “curing” and can add additional time to the tallying process.
Fourteen states and Washington D.C. also allow ballots postmarked by Election Day to be counted if they are received during a set post-election window, which can also add delays to final vote counts.
It will take significantly longer for the results of the election to be officially tabulated—or even projected by media outlets—in some states than in others.
When it comes to the media calling races, projections may take longer to come in cases when races are tight, and the winner does not become clear until nearly all the votes are counted.
“If there is a high margin of victory, they can make that projection sooner,” Wren Orey, who runs the Elections Project at the Bipartisan Policy Center, a policy think tank, tells TIME. “Whenever there's a very narrow margin of victory, that means that election officials need to process and report more results before a media outlet can be confident projecting a winner.”
In terms of the actual process of states counting votes, meanwhile, differences in speed can boil down to physical factors, such as the distance ballots must be transported before being counted. In states such as Alaska, for instance, vast and rural territories create delays for counting ballots. “There are sometimes ballots being flown back to Anchorage in order to be processed,” says Orey. They add that some states may also simply have more infrastructure to count ballots, including more machines, employees, and counting locations.
State laws governing how votes are cast and counted can also play a role in the timeline of election results. Alaska and Maine, for example, use ranked-choice voting, a process in which voters rank their top candidates instead of choosing one person for a position. Mann describes this method as a “more complicated process” in tight races, where ballots may need to be recounted due to one candidate not receiving an outright majority in the first or even subsequent rounds of counting.
“If no candidate has a majority on that first count, then they drop the candidate with the lowest number of votes, and they go through it again,” Mann explains.
Read more: 12 House Races That Forecasters See Going Different Ways
Other states, like Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, prohibit preparing mailed ballots for scanning until Election Day.
“Those are two of several states that don't start this process until the morning of Election Day, and they will have hundreds of thousands of ballots,” to prepare to be counted while running the polls at the same time, Mann says.
The process of confirming election results taking days or weeks, Mitchell says, is completely standard, and is not an indication of election fraud, which research and state audits have consistently shown to be extraordinarily rare.
“The thing that I would hammer home is not knowing an official result the day of the election, the day after the election, even a week after the election, is not evidence of fraud,” says Mitchell. “And to say so is to misconstrue and manipulate people.”

Crude oil prices fell Tuesday for a second consecutive session, as the market hopes the U.S. and Iran will reach a diplomatic settlement to the conflict that has disrupted global energy supplies for eight months.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures lost 37 cents to close at $96.09 a barrel after dipping below $95 earlier in the session. Brent crude , the international benchmark, shed $1.17 to settle at $103.60.
The move lower came after rumors circulated the U.S. and Iran were making progress toward a deal.
Oil sold off more than 7% on Monday after Washington and Tehran signaled they were both open to discussions to reach a settlement. President Donald Trump told reporters Tehran wants "to make a deal and that could happen."
Qatar is continuing to mediate talks between the U.S. and Iran, the Gulf state's foreign ministry said Tuesday. A delegation from Qatar held talks in Tehran in an effort to reach an agreement that prevents further escalation in the region and ends the U.S.-Iran conflict, the foreign ministry said.
However, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Emsaeil Baqaei said Tuesday that Tehran will not accept diplomacy based on coercion, according to the state-owned media outlet Islamic Republic News Agency . It was unclear where talks actual stand.
The market had been pricing in the risk of escalation after the U.S. midterm elections , as reports circulated that Washington was drafting plans for strikes on Iran. Crude prices gained more than 10% in October in response.
The situation in the Middle East remains volatile and there's still substantial risk that fighting could break out. Washington attacked Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday, U.S. officials told The Wall Street Journal, adding that the U.S. has been carrying out "limited strikes" against the country in recent weeks.
The military campaign against Iran has been kept deliberately low-profile to avoid signaling plans for a major escalation in fighting, the report said, quoting an unnamed official.
And commercial ships continue to come under attack in the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman. At least four ship attacks have been reported since the start of the month, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre.
Despite these attacks, the Trump administration has also been touting a possible diplomatic solution to the conflict, with Vice President JD Vance telling CNN, "The president and I both feel really good about the prospect of potentially coming to a negotiated settlement."
On Sunday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically," and prefers not to use military force.
High oil prices have contributed substantially to inflation and high gasoline prices in the U.S., which have become a cause of concern for Trump ahead of the midterm elections.
Last week, two Federal Reserve presidents said interest rates will need to move higher to rein in inflation. Higher rates generally crimp growth and raise costs for consumers, but help to bring down inflation.

Four oil tankers were destroyed after hitting naval mines in an area south of the Strait of Hormuz proscribed by Iran as prohibited for navigation, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Wednesday, as attacks on vessels in the region intensify while crude oil flows have dipped from recent highs.
The four tankers are still ablaze, while two other vessels have been seized, the Revolutionary Guards said.
While flows have recovered substantially from the lows in the spring, the security situation in and near the Strait of Hormuz has actually deteriorated, with a higher number of attacks on tankers in recent weeks.
Following a post-war peak in September, exports of crude oil, condensate, and fuels from the Middle East slipped to 17.1 million barrels per day (bpd) in October, down from 18.9 million bpd in September, according to data from Vortexa cited by Reuters .
“October data shows Middle East seaborne oil exports have pulled back slightly from recent post-war highs on heightened risks in the Strait of Hormuz,” George Morris, an analyst at Vortexa, said in comments reported by the publication.
Kpler has tracked a 1-million-bpd drop in total crude oil and condensate exports. Crude and condensate flows through the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, and the Gulf of Oman are estimated, provisionally, to have dropped to 16.1 million bpd in October, from 17.09 million bpd in September.
However, the tanker-tracking services caution that the numbers could be revised up as more details on shipments, especially shuttle shipments, emerge in the coming days.
Oil flows from the Middle East region have materially increased since the lows in April and May, but the heightened security concerns and intensified attacks, mines, and other explosions and incidents are making tracking shipments difficult. Tanker-trackers increasingly rely on satellite imagery to confirm movements because vessels are often switching off transponders to avoid detection when transiting the Strait of Hormuz.

McDonald's on Wednesday reported mixed quarterly results as traffic to its U.S. restaurants fell, leading to a slight decline in domestic same-store sales.
The fast-food giant reported a 0.2% decrease in sales at its U.S. restaurants that have been open at least 13 months. Even so, the segment performed better than the 0.5% decline that Wall Street anticipated, according to a survey of analysts by StreetAccount.
At the company's investor day in September, executives said that same-store sales in July and August were slightly negative but they expected September to return to same-store sales growth.
"In the U.S., we're encouraged by improvement as the quarter progressed following our intervention on value," McDonald's CEO Chris Kempczinski said in a statement.
Kempczinski said in August that the company's U.S. business was falling short on execution, particularly on the implementation of its value offerings. Like many restaurants, McDonald's has leaned into discounts to attract budget-conscious diners over the last two years.
Shares of the company rose more than 2% in premarket trading.
Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
The company reported third-quarter net income of $2.49 billion, or $3.51 per share, up from $2.28 billion, or $3.18 per share, a year earlier.
Excluding restructuring charges and other items, McDonald's earned $3.57 per share.
Net revenue rose 1% to $7.16 billion.
The company's same-store sales rose 1.5%, lifted by its international segments. That topped analysts' expectations of a 1.3% increase, according to StreetAccount.
McDonald's international developmental licensed markets business, which includes Japan and China, reported same-store sales growth of 4.2%. Wall Street was forecasting same-store sales to rise 2.1% for the division, based on StreetAccount estimates.
The company's international operated division, which includes top markets like Australia and Germany, saw same-store sales growth of 1.4%. Still, the business underperformed Wall Street's expectations. Analysts were projecting same-store sales would rise 2.1%, according to StreetAccount. France was a weak spot, McDonald's said.

articles.title_orig: Hackers use n-day exploits in zero-click attacks on iOS, Android devices
articles.title_zh: Hackers use n-day exploits in zero-click attacks on iOS, Android devices
articles.content_orig:
A large-scale watering hole attack associated with Russian hackers has been targeting iOS and Android users visiting compromised sites or fake ones impersonating legitimate portals.
The campaign used multiple high-profile websites in the U.S., Ukraine, the Czech Republic, and Bulgaria that delivered the same payload for profiling visitors and their devices.
This initial stage allows the attacker to determine the browser version to deploy "platform-specific n-day exploit chains without user interaction."
Researchers at cybersecurity company Sekoia attribute the operation with moderate-to-high confidence to APT29 (aka Midnight Blizzard), a Russian threat group that was recently linked to hotel WiFi attacks .
Based on their findings, compromised legitimate sites belong to a Ukrainian gas producer, a U.S. chemical industry trade association, and a Bulgarian military-related site.
Lookalike domains impersonated the official America250 site and Raffles London at The OWO hotel, relaying content from the real sites in an adversary-in-the-middle attack model.
The researchers also discovered that the threat actor had compromised Ukrainian web analytics service Plerdy and modified its SEO tracker, which was loaded by thousands of websites, mostly in Ukraine, between August 27 and September 3.
In all cases, the initial payload was JavaScript code that profiled website visitors to determine their devices and browser versions. The command-and-control (C2) server then pushed the correct exploit chain.
According to Sekoia, the threat actors exploited the following vulnerabilities to extract cookies, messaging app databases, and credentials:
The researchers identified four other vulnerabilities in unreachable code or alternate exploit paths, but they were not used in the analyzed chains.
CVE-2025-43529 is linked to the “DarkSword” exploit kit , first documented in March, and leveraged in attacks since at least November 2025 by multiple threat groups.
Sekoia says that none of the payloads APT29 used in these attacks established persistence, allowing a device reboot to stop the malicious activity until visiting a compromised site again.
Regarding its attribution to APT29, Sekoia notes similarities to past watering-hole operations by the same threat group, infrastructure overlaps, and a compromised site that a partner linked to a 2025 APT29 campaign.
Apple and Google have patched all flaws targeted in this campaign, with fixes even reaching older iOS releases , so users are recommended to apply the latest available security updates for their devices.

articles.content_orig:
The Democratic Party has regained control of the lower chamber of the United States Congress, winning the House of Representatives.
Late on Tuesday night local time, the House result was called in favour of the left-wing party.
Democrats needed to gain five seats to flip the chamber. Republicans have held a majority in the House since the 2022 midterms, during the presidency of Democrat Joe Biden.
The outgoing 119th House has 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, one independent and two vacancies.
All 435 seats in the House were up for grabs in the election. A term in the House lasts only two years, compared with six for the Senate.
The Democrats’ victory in the House means their party leader in the chamber, Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, will likely be selected as the speaker, the chamber’s top officer.
That position would make Jeffries the third in line for the US presidency, should the president and the vice president be removed from office.
He would also be the first Black person to serve in the role. He will replace outgoing Republican Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana, who has held the post since 2023.
Democrats had been widely projected to regain control of the House, leveraging backlash to the second administration of President Donald Trump, which saw record-low approval ratings in the weeks leading up to the midterms.
For the last two years, Trump’s Republican Party has held a political “trifecta” in Washington, DC, with control of the presidency and both chambers of Congress. The 120th Congress is slated to be sworn in on January 3, 2027.
Democrats swept Republican-held House seats on their way to retaking the chamber.
In Iowa, Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott unseated Republican Zach Nunn in the state’s 3rd Congressional District.
In Virginia, Democrat Elaine Luria won a tight race against Republican incumbent Jen Kiggans, while in Pennsylvania’s 10th Congressional District, Democrat Janelle Stelson unseated seven-term Republican Scott Perry.
Meanwhile, Democrat incumbents Ilhan Omar and Ro Khanna sailed to victory, holding on to their seats in Minnesota and California.
Reacting to the Democratic wave, former President Barack Obama said the results showed voters wanted leaders who would bring people together and offer solutions to the problems they face.
“Tonight, the American people sent a clear message,” Obama wrote on X. He praised candidates who ran in areas long considered difficult for Democrats to win and urged supporters to keep organising during Trump’s remaining two years in office.
Senator Bernie Sanders said Democratic control of both chambers would allow the party to “hold Trump accountable”.
He urged Democrats to tackle income and wealth inequality. “We must aggressively fight for working families. No more excuses,” Sanders said.
Even Trump issued rare praise for the Democratic campaign in an interview with Fox News.
“I think the Democrats did a good job. I really do. I think they did a good job. They fought hard,” the president said.

articles.title_orig: Gold, silver and precious metals prices jump, dollar dips as Democrats take control of Congress
articles.title_zh: Gold, silver and precious metals prices jump, dollar dips as Democrats take control of Congress
articles.content_orig:
Precious metals saw strong gains on Wednesday morning, while the value of the dollar fell, following the U.S. midterm elections.
Spot gold was 2.83% higher at $4,039.59 an ounce by 7:56 a.m. ET, while spot silver jumped 4.32% to trade at $51.9235 per ounce.
Front-month gold futures added 2.8% to trade at $4,050.80, while silver futures were up 4.61% at $52.045.
Other metals seeing notable gains on Wednesday morning included platinum , which jumped 3.43% to trade at $1,464.60, and palladium, which was 6.21% higher at $991.50.
The moves came as vote counting continued in the midterms, with the Democrats projected to have won control of the House and multiple governors' offices also turning blue.
U.S. stock futures broadly fell as the results came in, while Treasury yields also moved lower . Oil prices were marginally higher, while the U.S. dollar index shed around 0.3%.
Rhona O'Connell, head of market analysis for EMEA and Asia at StoneX, said in a note on Tuesday that if the Democrats won dual Congressional control, gold should find support as rates and the dollar would likely come under pressure.
She said it would result in "fiscal brinkmanship, institutional friction, both leading to uncertainty," adding that "the Iran war and a weaker dollar would compete with [the] impact of [a] hawkish Fed."
"Less fiscal stimulus argues for lower long yields and a softer dollar, offset by debt-limit premia in bills and a Fed leaning towards another hike," she said.
Both gold and silver enjoyed record-breaking rallies in 2025, surging 66% and 135% respectively over the course of the year as investors sought safe haven assets amid geopolitical uncertainty and broader market volatility.
But the momentum has come undone this year, with rising inflation, surging bond yields and hawkish central banks removing support from the metals. Gold is down more than 7% year-to-date, while silver has tumbled almost 28%.
Spot gold rose on Monday as oil prices retreated, and is now on course for a weekly rise of around 3.7%.
Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com, said in a Tuesday note that the recovery remains fragile.
"The challenge for precious metals is that geopolitical uncertainty is not automatically translating into safe-haven demand when investors are also concerned about restrictive monetary policy," she said. "They also face the risk of liquidation during sharp equity selloffs, as investors sell profitable or liquid positions to raise cash."

The question of “how much oil is getting out of the Middle East” has come up time and again. Often with the additional question of “if so much oil is getting out, why are prices still so high?”
We tried to address that in length last week, but let’s re-summarize as it is important. In a nutshell, why these reports are misleading:
Let’s just start with an updated version of last weekend’s ( SOX ) (semiconductor index) chart.
Markets initially bounced off of the 200-day moving average, but on Friday, they retested that level and failed. It is often the third retest that is the problem, so a bounce again is quite possible, but breaking the 200-DMA rarely is a good thing.
The Nasdaq 100 is solidly through its 100-DMA and is about 1.6% from testing its own 200-DMA. On Friday, the S&P 500 just broke its 100-DMA for the first time since November 2025. The 200-DMA is 3.5% away on the S&P 500, which should be support.
We are resorting to technicals more than usual because:
From what I see anecdotally and through some simple charts I like to use, the market is not exhibiting strength, and the risk is to further downside.
One positive is credit markets didn’t suffer as badly as stocks on Friday (spreads did not finish at their wides) and none of my indicators for “disorderly” selling pressure have triggered. I am watching those triggers as that is a risk that is still in play.
I remain concerned about the abundance of leveraged ETFs focused on the chip space (with ( SOXL ) being the largest). These amplify moves in both directions. While SOXL had some inflows on Friday, it would have had to sell about $8 billion of stocks into the close, without inflows. This added pressure makes it difficult to separate valuation from mechanically forced buying and selling.
With these indices all potentially exposed to some weak technicals, that makes me very cautious.
The chip sector is crucial for markets and for the economy. A degree of caution seems warranted at the moment, though we have all seen these markets turn on a dime.
I will wait to see how Tuesday plays out. We have become accustomed to polls being inaccurate. Even betting markets failed in Brazil, which we avoided in an otherwise broad cross section of geopolitical risks and opportunities last Monday on CNBC . European stocks did outperform the U.S. last week, despite all the headlines.
I will be watching almost as closely (or more closely) how political leaders respond to the election results. That may be more telling for markets than the results themselves.
I do have a small concern that we could be in for more volatility from the elections than people are pricing in.
The start of this week won’t be about bond yields. The Federal Reserve, I think, sent a message it will hike if necessary, but would only do so kicking and screaming. If anything, yields will respond to signs of economic growth or slowdown (driven primarily by the compute spend).
Credit outperformed stocks last week. While stocks finished at their lows in many cases, credit was not at the widest levels. This is very good. It is also good for equities that credit has been weak, but the weakness is targeted and the market is still trading in an orderly fashion. Credit not breaking (which remains a risk) provides strong support for stocks.

articles.title_orig: Iran says US reply to Hormuz plan ‘unconvincing’; Trump confirms strikes
articles.title_zh: Iran says US reply to Hormuz plan ‘unconvincing’; Trump confirms strikes
articles.content_orig:
Iran has called the US response to its seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz “unconvincing” as US President Donald Trump confirmed launching strikes on an Iranian island near the strategic waterway.
The developments on Tuesday came as Qatar stepped up diplomatic efforts to avert a renewed war between the US and Iran and as another oil tanker was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz.
The indirect talks centre on an Iranian proposal to reopen the waterway over two days, if the US meets Tehran’s seven demands, including the lifting of sanctions and ending a US naval blockade.
Despite reports of progress in recent days, Mohsen Rezaei , the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said on Tuesday that Washington’s response had fallen short.
“America’s response to Iran’s rights and demands was not convincing, and they must fully and explicitly address Iran’s seven conditions and act upon them,” he wrote on X.
“Only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened.”
His post came after Majed al-Ansari, a spokesperson for Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said that talks were continuing and that both sides “remain committed to the negotiation process “.
He said Qatar was facilitating the “real-time exchange of proposals between” the US and Iran.
In Washington, DC, Trump confirmed the US had struck Iran early on Tuesday, telling Fox News that the strikes had targeted an anti-aircraft facility.
He described the operation as a “minor attack” and said it “wasn’t war”.
“They built an anti-aircraft facility. It took them about two months. We watched it get built. As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night,” he said.
Iranian media said the strikes hit Qeshm Island in the Gulf near the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier in the day, US officials told US media that the strikes had been “defensive” and followed Iranian fire at an American aircraft.
The strikes came as US media, citing US officials, reported that Central Command had prepared plans for strikes that could begin as early as Wednesday, after the midterm elections, when three American aircraft carriers would be in the region.
The crucial elections could cost Trump’s Republicans control of both the House and the Senate, and fears have grown that Trump could carry out a threatened attack on Iran once the vote is over.
US media have previously reported that the planned campaign would be short and intense.
Trump meanwhile repeated warnings of further military action on Tuesday, saying, “I’m not looking to … kill lots of people” and “If we have to, we’ll have to.”
In an earlier interview with the Financial Times, he suggested he was content with the state of the stand-off with Iran. “We seem to be getting everything we want,” the paper quoted him as saying in a six-minute telephone interview.
Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, meanwhile ordered the military at the weekend to respond to any threat immediately and without geographical limits, and to update its list of targets.
Iranian officials have suggested that European countries and undersea cables in the Gulf could be targeted.
As officials weighed the possibility of escalation, commercial shipping came under further attack .
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed on Wednesday that four oil tankers were destroyed after striking naval mines while attempting to pass through a prohibited shipping lane south of the Strait of Hormuz.
The tankers remained ablaze following the explosions, the IRGC said in a statement carried by the official IRNA news agency. Two other vessels were detained for violating shipping restrictions, it added.
Earlier, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported that two unidentified projectiles struck a tanker’s engine room about 14 nautical miles (26km) northeast of Oman’s coastal village of Limah on Tuesday. No casualties were reported.
It could not be independently verified whether the incidents reported by UKMTO and the IRGC were linked.
The IRGC also claimed its air defence forces shot down a US-made MQ-9 drone over the strait at 4.30am local time (01:00GMT), describing it as the 56th such aircraft it had downed.
The statement said the operations were carried out by the IRGC’s naval and aerospace forces, which had inflicted “heavy blows on the enemy”.
John Mearsheimer, a US political scientist, questioned whether another short bombing campaign could achieve Washington’s objectives, warning that Iranian retaliation could draw the US into a longer confrontation.
“If the 40-day bombing campaign didn’t work, how is the three-day bombing campaign going to work?” he asked in a video commentary, referring to the initial US-Israeli air campaign and proposals for a shorter renewed offensive.
He argued that an Iranian response could prompt further US escalation, increasing the damage to the global economy.

AI stocks ​were quick to slide. That in turn put the dollar under pressure, while cryptocurrencies also fell at the prospect of stronger regulations. Bonds, though, found favour as investors sought safer assets.
"Tighter regulatory scrutiny of technology and AI companies along with the higher likelihood of political gridlock beckon with a Democrat sweep," said Prashant Newnaha, senior rates strategist at TD Securities in Singapore.
The AI boom has helped propel global markets in recent years, driven by heavy spending from tech giants racing to build data centres and expand computing capacity. That has ‌left investors acutely sensitive to anything that could derail the ⁠technology's rapid expansion.
The election outcome could also hold broad implications for the US fiscal outlook as well as sectors such as defence, healthcare and banking.
S&P 500 futures were last down 0.35% while Nasdaq futures skidded more than 2% before cutting losses to trade down 0.5%. ⁠European futures were down 0.4%, having slid 1.5% earlier.
"Looks like investors are buying the dip after the initial knee-jerk selloff," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo. "The blue sweep hasn't changed, but markets may be recognising that political gridlock doesn't necessarily mean weaker corporate earnings."
In Asia, the bulk of selling was in AI stocks, with chipmakers Samsung, SK Hynix and TSMC sliding ​sharply ​before cutting losses. The KOSPI was last slightly higher after dropping 3% earlier.
George Efstathopoulos, portfolio manager ​and co-head of multi-asset research at Fidelity International, said he had ‌reduced overall equity exposure and dialled up exposure in defensive sectors like utilities, but thinks now is a good time to gradually rotate back into tech.
"The midterms are a clearing event that can allow investors to focus on sectors where fundamentals and pricing have diverged. Technology is one of them."
INVESTORS RUSH FOR SAFETY OF BONDS
Treasuries rallied as investors expect gridlock in Washington to cut government spending. AI regulation could also slow growth and reduce the need for rate hikes.
The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note fell 6 basis points to 4.906%, pushing the dollar sharply lower. [FRX/] [US/]
"Bonds are coming out as the clear winner as markets put the AI trade on the chopping block ‌and embrace the higher possibility that further tax cuts are put on ice and government spending ​slows," said TD Securities' Newnaha.
Kim Seok-hwan, an analyst at Mirae Asset Securities, said the Democrats' victory in ​Texas is likely to weigh on chip stocks, raising fears of tighter ​curbs on AI data-centre development in one of the fastest-growing markets for computing infrastructure in the US.
"If Texas declares a moratorium on data ‌centres, as New York did, projects could face further delays," Kim ​said. "Today's market reaction is clearly reflecting concerns ​and uncertainty over these issues."
In currencies, the dollar slid broadly against major peers. The euro rose 0.5% to $1.1249, while sterling firmed 0.37% to $1.3464. That left the dollar index 0.37% lower at 101.34. [FRX/]
The yen and the Swiss franc — both safe-haven currencies — notched up the biggest gains. The yen was 0.7% stronger at 157.55 ​per US dollar, while the Swiss franc firmed almost 0.8% ‌to 0.8144 per US dollar.
In the oil market, prices were choppy on Wednesday after sliding to a four-week low in the previous session as ​investors weighed talks to end the wars in Ukraine and Iran against worries that recent attacks in both conflicts could further disrupt supplies. [O/R]

articles.title_orig: Ecologist fights for custody of badger he rescued as a cub
articles.title_zh: Ecologist fights for custody of badger he rescued as a cub
articles.content_orig:
An ecologist in the Scottish Borders is fighting to be allowed to keep a badger that he saved from starvation.
Graeme Wilson was called out to help the cub, called Harriet, in April after she was found in a cattle trough 100m (300ft) from her sett.
Wilson nursed the badger back to health but believes she was hand-reared prior to this, and it would be impossible to return her to the wild.
NatureScot - which turned down his application for an educational licence to keep the animal - said it was continuing talks to try to find a "pragmatic solution".
Wilson runs GW Ecology, a small independent rescue and rehabilitation service at his home in Denholm.
It carries out surveys to determine whether protected species are present on the sites of proposed property developments.
He also leads bat walks, workshops and holds educational events about wildlife and how to protect it.
Wilson describes himself as an "experienced and trained wildlife rehabber" who has cared for a variety of wildlife over the years.
He argues that an educational licence could allow him to support public understanding of badgers, wildlife rescue and caring for a protected species.
He said that after rescuing Harriet,  it quickly became evident to him that she could not go back to where he found her.
Wilson added: "It was almost second nature when she saw the bottle.
"I have cared for injured badgers before and never have I seen something like it.
"It was clear then she couldn't be released back into the wild."
He said NatureScot, the public body responsible for Scotland's natural heritage and wildlife, had told him she should be returned to the wild or sent to a zoo.
However, he believes that releasing Harriet into the wild would only result in her being hurt or killed.
He said: "Badgers are companion animals, they are a social animal and unfortunately for Harriet she has decided that humans are her social group.
"Can you imagine Harriet approaching someone on a dog walk or in the street?
"There is only one way that would end."
He said a zoo would also be unsuitable for Harriet, arguing she would become lonely and suffer unnecessary distress.
"Harriet's upbringing means she needs human interaction, not to be put behind glass and stared at," he said.
Wilson said he would keeping fighting to hold on to Harriet.
However, he admitted there may not be a lot he can do, despite having the support of several badger rescue groups in Scotland.
Police Scotland has been made aware of the situation.
NatureScot said talks were ongoing to try to find a way to resolve the issue.
"We are continuing discussions with Mr Wilson and other relevant organisations to try and find a pragmatic solution to this individual situation," said a spokesperson.
"The welfare of the badger is, of course, key while we consider the circumstances of the case."
Scottish SPCA advice is that any badger cub discovered outside its sett before it is about 12 weeks old - or about the size of a domestic cat - is likely to need help.
It said any member of the public coming across a sick or injured badger should not attempt to hold or touch the animal until one of its rescue officers arrives.
"Badgers can become aggressive if they are in pain or feel threatened; they can give a nasty bite and their sharp claws could cause serious injury, if you try to catch it," it said.
"You should also contact us if you find a badger during daylight hours as they may be struggling."

Stock futures were mixed early on Wednesday as traders speculated that Democrats were headed for majority control of Congress and some key gubernatorial wins in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections .

The Democratic Party is projected to win both chambers of Congress, according to The Associated Press. Hinojosa has pledged a moratorium on data centers in the key tech hub.
Democrats securing a sizable majority in the House and Senate — the so-called blue wave scenario — would pressure the market and especially stocks related to the artificial intelligence buildout, according to some on Wall Street. Investors fear a big Democratic win could mean more restrictions on data centers nationwide. AI-linked stocks have already pulled back in recent weeks on concern about a slowing pace in data-center spending.
Big Tech shares Microsoft , Amazon and Nvidia were all trading lower in overnight trading on Robinhood.
Elon Musk's SpaceX was down 4.6% on Robinhood, while Tesla shares were down 4.1%. Data center play CoreWeave was down 3.2% in Robinhood overnight trading, while Alphabet was some 0.6% lower.
Equities "trended lower as it's looked more likely that Democrats are going to pick up the House and most likely the Senate," said Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise Financial, Tuesday evening as futures were pulling back.

Renewable shares like solar stocks traded higher in the post-market on speculation a Democratic majority in Congress would halt policies by President Donald Trump taken against the industry. The Invesco Solar ETF was up 3% in Robinhood trading.

Leveraged traders trimmed holdings to a one-year low this week, while new stock-account openings dropped by more than 30 per cent in October
Chinese investors refrained from bets on stocks this week, even as state support unfolded after Beijing unveiled a litany of measures to shore up confidence in the world’s second-largest equity market.
Leveraged traders trimmed their holdings to a one-year low this week, while new stock-account openings dropped by more than 30 per cent in October, according to official data. The retreat in retail enthusiasm contrasted with the government ramping up efforts to prop up stocks, including liquidity injections through two monetary tools and reported suspensions of new share sales to keep a lid on supply.
The divergence illustrates investors’ unease over whether the latest bout of government interventions will drive sustained gains in stocks, which are grappling with weak domestic demand and the fallout of a rout in AI stocks in the US. Investment banks including Bank of America and Macquarie said that state intervention might stabilise sentiment, but would fall short of fuelling a fresh rally.

articles.title_orig: Oil rises on Iran war uncertainty after Trump's Republicans face election rout
articles.title_zh: Oil rises on Iran war uncertainty after Trump's Republicans face election rout
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices fell Tuesday for a second consecutive session, as the market hopes the U.S. and Iran will reach a diplomatic settlement to the conflict that has disrupted global energy supplies for eight months.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures lost 37 cents to close at $96.09 a barrel after dipping below $95 earlier in the session. Brent crude , the international benchmark, shed $1.17 to settle at $103.60.
The move lower came after rumors circulated the U.S. and Iran were making progress toward a deal.
Oil sold off more than 7% on Monday after Washington and Tehran signaled they were both open to discussions to reach a settlement. President Donald Trump told reporters Tehran wants "to make a deal and that could happen."
Qatar is continuing to mediate talks between the U.S. and Iran, the Gulf state's foreign ministry said Tuesday. A delegation from Qatar held talks in Tehran in an effort to reach an agreement that prevents further escalation in the region and ends the U.S.-Iran conflict, the foreign ministry said.
However, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Emsaeil Baqaei said Tuesday that Tehran will not accept diplomacy based on coercion, according to the state-owned media outlet Islamic Republic News Agency . It was unclear where talks actual stand.
The market had been pricing in the risk of escalation after the U.S. midterm elections , as reports circulated that Washington was drafting plans for strikes on Iran. Crude prices gained more than 10% in October in response.
The situation in the Middle East remains volatile and there's still substantial risk that fighting could break out. Washington attacked Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday, U.S. officials told The Wall Street Journal, adding that the U.S. has been carrying out "limited strikes" against the country in recent weeks.
The military campaign against Iran has been kept deliberately low-profile to avoid signaling plans for a major escalation in fighting, the report said, quoting an unnamed official.
And commercial ships continue to come under attack in the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman. At least four ship attacks have been reported since the start of the month, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre.
Despite these attacks, the Trump administration has also been touting a possible diplomatic solution to the conflict, with Vice President JD Vance telling CNN, "The president and I both feel really good about the prospect of potentially coming to a negotiated settlement."
On Sunday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically," and prefers not to use military force.
High oil prices have contributed substantially to inflation and high gasoline prices in the U.S., which have become a cause of concern for Trump ahead of the midterm elections.
Last week, two Federal Reserve presidents said interest rates will need to move higher to rein in inflation. Higher rates generally crimp growth and raise costs for consumers, but help to bring down inflation.
— CNBC's Priyanka Salve contributed to this report.
